plain: A folder named .codex where Codex keeps project settings, rules and custom agents. Your home folder has one too, for your own settings.
Typing @ before a file path in your message to add that file to Codex's context at once.
Building a site so that people with disabilities, such as blind or deaf users, can use it.
An error that means another program already uses the port you asked for. Stop that program or choose another port.
An AI program that plans steps and uses tools on its own to finish a task, instead of only answering questions.
A Markdown file of instructions that Codex reads before it works. Codex looks for AGENTS.md files from the project root down.
Commands that Codex may run without an approval prompt. Rules in .codex/rules set them.
To replace your latest commit with a new one, for example to fix its message or add a forgotten file.
A short function written in place, usually without a name. In JavaScript it is often an arrow function (=>); in Python, a lambda.
A secret code that lets a program use a service as you. Treat it like a password and never paste it into a chat.
The basic set of 128 characters: English letters, digits and common symbols. An ASCII name has no accents or other letters.
Code that starts a slow task and lets the program do other work while it waits.
Windows paths use a backslash (\) between folders; macOS and Linux use a forward slash (/). Many Windows tools accept both.
A new version that still works with the code, files or settings made for the older version.
A way to write binary data, such as an image, using only letters, digits and a few symbols. It is not encryption.
A widely used shell on Linux. It is also available on macOS, and on Windows through Git Bash.
A file that is not plain text, such as an image. A compiled, ready-to-run program is also called a binary.
A Git command that shows, for each line of a file, the commit and author that last changed it.
Standard code or text that many projects need and that is copied with few changes, such as a project's starting files.
The slowest part of a system. It limits how fast everything else can go.
GitHub rules that limit what can happen to a branch, such as requiring a pull request or blocking force pushes.
A file that a build or test run produces and saves, such as a compiled app or a test report.
The step that turns your source code into the files that run or are published, for example by compiling and bundling.
A tool that combines many source files into a few files for the browser. The output is called a bundle.
A stored copy of a result, kept so the program can answer faster next time without repeating the work.
A function you give to other code so that it can call it later, for example when a download finishes.
Treating capital and small letters as different. On Linux, README.md and readme.md are two files; Windows and macOS usually treat them as one name.
Content delivery network: servers around the world that keep copies of your site's files and send them from the nearest one.
A digital file that proves a website's identity, so that the browser can trust the connection. HTTPS needs one.
A Git command that copies one chosen commit from another branch onto the branch you are on.
The AI model that Codex uses to read your project and decide what to do. /status shows which model is in use.
A program you use by typing commands in a terminal instead of clicking buttons. Codex has a CLI.
Computers run by a provider such as AWS, Google or Microsoft, which you rent over the internet instead of owning.
The older Windows command line. Its prompt has no PS in front, and it runs different commands from PowerShell.
A development environment that GitHub runs for you in the cloud, opened from a repository.
A person you give access to your GitHub repository so that they can push changes to it.
A list of the commands you typed before. In a terminal, the Up arrow key brings back the last one.
The list of all commits in a repository, in order. The git log command shows it.
A program that translates the code you wrote into a form the computer can run. Compiling happens before the program runs.
A reusable piece of a user interface, such as a button or a menu, written once and used in many places.
An isolated environment where a program runs with its own files and settings, apart from your normal ones. Docker is a common tool for it.
A saved package of files and settings from which containers are started. Docker builds and stores images.
In an AI chat, all the text the model can use right now: your messages, files it has read and command output.
Preparing or releasing every change automatically after its tests pass. Delivery waits for approval; deployment publishes at once. CI/CD joins this with CI.
A browser security rule: a web page may read data from another site only if that site's server allows it.
A task that a computer runs automatically on a schedule. Cron is the scheduler on macOS and Linux.
An attack where another website makes your browser send an unwanted request to a site where you are signed in.
A command-line tool that sends a web request and prints the response, often used to test an API.
An older way to add your own prompt: a Markdown file in ~/.codex/prompts/. Codex has deprecated it, and skills are the new way.
A public ID, such as CVE-2024-12345, for one known security flaw in software. Security alerts often cite it.
A program that keeps running in the background without a window, waiting to do work, such as a database server.
An extra structure that lets a database find rows by a column faster. It uses more storage and slows writes slightly.
Put a new version of an app on the server where users can reach it.
Still works, but its authors advise against using it because it will be removed later.
A state where Git points at one commit instead of a branch. New commits made there can be lost unless you create a branch.
A package needed only while developing, such as a test tool, and not when the app runs for users.
Another word for a folder. Terminals and documentation usually say directory.
The part of a computer that stores files permanently, such as an SSD. Files stay there when the computer is turned off.
A tool that packages an app with everything it needs into a container, so it runs the same way on any computer with Docker.
A pull request marked as not ready for review yet. GitHub does not let you merge a draft until it is marked ready.
Running a program in a mode that only shows what it would do, without changing anything.
A test that uses the whole app the way a user would, for example by clicking through it in a browser.
An error that means a file or folder was not found. Check the spelling and which folder you are in.
Code that waits for an event, such as a click, and runs when it happens.
A file that the computer can run as a program, such as an .exe file on Windows.
Step-by-step reasoning that the model does before it answers. The amount is a setting, such as model_reasoning_effort in config.toml.
A small add-on that gives an editor such as VS Code new features.
A branch made to build one feature or fix, then merged into the main branch when it is done.
Settings that say who may read, change or run a file. On macOS and Linux, the chmod command changes them.
The way a computer organises and stores files and folders on a disk.
An extra word starting with - or -- after a command, such as -p, that changes how the command runs.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails when nothing in the code changed.
A column that holds the primary key of a row in another table, so that the two rows are linked.
A small block at the very top of a Markdown file, between two lines of three dashes, that holds settings such as paths.
A script that Git runs automatically at a set moment, for example before a commit is made.
Git Large File Storage: an extension that keeps big files outside normal Git history and stores small pointers instead.
A fixed name for one commit, such as v1.0.0, often used to mark a release.
A GitHub page for one version of a project, built on a Git tag, with release notes and downloadable files.
A pattern with wildcards that matches many file names at once, such as *.md for every Markdown file.
A program you use with windows, buttons and a mouse instead of typed commands.
Your personal folder on the computer. It usually holds your Desktop, Documents and Downloads folders, and Codex's own ~/.codex folder.
A handler, usually a command, that Codex runs at a set moment, such as before a tool use. Use /hooks to review them.
When you save a file, the dev server updates the page in your browser by itself, without a manual refresh.
A program for writing and running code, such as VS Code or a JetBrains editor. Codex has an IDE extension.
Safe to run more than once: running it twice gives the same result as running it once.
Spaces or tabs at the start of a line. In Python they show which lines belong together.
A loop that never ends, so the program never finishes. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.
A test that checks that several parts of a program work together, for example the code and its database.
A tool where a team lists bugs and tasks, such as GitHub Issues or Jira.
To go through the items of a list one at a time. A loop does this.
A company whose code editors include IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm and WebStorm.
A plain-text format for storing data as named values inside curly braces. Many settings files use it.
JSON Web Token: signed text that a server gives you after login. You send it back with requests to prove who you are.
The date after which an AI model has no built-in knowledge, so it may not know newer tools or versions.
The waiting time between sending a request and receiving the answer.
The position number of an item in a list. In most languages the first item is at index 0, not 1.
A server that shares incoming visits between several copies of an app.
Long-term support: a version that gets bug and security fixes for longer than normal versions, such as Node.js LTS.
A person who looks after an open-source project and decides which changes are accepted.
A plain text format where # makes a heading and - makes a list item. Files end in .md.
A catalog of plugins. Codex installs plugins from the marketplaces you have set up.
A saved script that changes the structure of a database, such as adding a column, and can be run in order on any copy.
To shrink code by removing spaces and comments and shortening names, so it downloads faster but is harder to read.
A fake stand-in for a real part, such as a web service, used in tests so that they are fast and predictable.
A Python error that means it cannot find a package you imported. Install it, or check that the right environment is active.
One repository that holds the code of several projects or packages.
A Python error that means you used a name, such as a variable or function, that does not exist yet. Often a typo.
A program that runs JavaScript outside a browser, on your computer or a server. Its installer includes the npm package manager.
The folder where npm puts the packages a project uses. It is large and generated, so it is normally not committed to Git.
Running codex exec once without the interactive screen. It prints the answer and exits, so scripts can call it.
A database value that means no value is stored. It is not zero or an empty string. Python code reads it as None.
A standard that lets you sign in to one app with an account from another, such as GitHub, without sharing your password.
A value that groups related named data, and sometimes actions, in one place, such as a user with a name and an e-mail.
The main software that runs a computer and its programs, such as Windows, macOS or Linux.
A library that lets code use database tables as objects and writes the SQL for you.
A library in your project for which the package manager knows a newer version.
Code that other people wrote and shared, which you install into your project, usually with a package manager.
An AGENTS.md file placed in a sub-folder. Codex reads it when it works in that folder or in a folder below it.
The main data in a request or response, such as the JSON you send to an API, not the headers.
A line in a .codex/rules file that says a command may run (allow), must ask first (prompt) or is blocked (forbidden).
Process ID: the number your computer gives to each running program. You can use it to stop that program.
In CI, a series of automated steps that run in order, such as build, test and deploy. If one fails, later steps usually stop.
A package that adds skills and MCP servers to Codex in one install.
Extra code that adds a feature to older browsers that do not have it.
A database that runs as its own server and handles many users writing at the same time.
The built-in Windows shell and terminal. Its prompt starts with PS. Its commands differ from CMD.
A Git hook that runs before a commit is made. If it fails, Git stops the commit.
In JavaScript, an object that stands for a result that will arrive later, such as a finished download.
The text you send to an AI tool to ask for something, such as 'fix the failing test'.
A programming language known for readable code, used for scripts, data work and web apps. Files end in .py.
A bug where the result depends on which of two actions happens first, and the order changes from run to run.
The fast, temporary memory that a running program uses. Its contents are lost when the program ends or the computer turns off.
A JavaScript library for building web pages from reusable parts called components.
To replay your commits on top of another commit. It creates new commits and rewrites history.
A pattern written in a special syntax to find or match text, such as every e-mail address in a file.
An interactive prompt where you type one line of code and see its result at once. Typing python starts one.
A value, such as an API key, stored encrypted in a repository's GitHub settings so that workflows can use it.
A named group of GitHub rules for branches or tags. Several rulesets can apply to the same branch at once.
Software that runs programs written in a language, such as Node.js for JavaScript. At runtime means while a program is running.
A restricted area that limits which files and network access a command can use. Codex sets it with sandbox_mode in config.toml.
To generate a project's starting files and folders with a tool, instead of writing them by hand.
How well a system keeps working when it gets more users or more data.
A folder you create only to practise in, so that mistakes cannot harm a real project.
A file of commands or code that a program runs from start to finish, such as setup.sh or build.py.
Software development kit: a ready-made library that helps you use a service from your own code.
A crash, mostly in programs written in C or C++, when the program uses memory it is not allowed to use.
Turning data held in memory into text or bytes that can be saved or sent, for example into JSON.
A way of hosting code where the provider runs it only when needed and you do not manage a server yourself.
A settings file in TOML format. Codex keeps its options there. The project one is .codex/config.toml.
The long code of letters and digits that identifies one Git commit. Git commands accept its first few characters.
A short custom name that stands for a longer command. In PowerShell, ls is an alias for Get-ChildItem.
A command you type inside Codex that starts with /, such as /clear, /resume or /status.
A SQL operation that combines rows from two tables by matching a shared value, such as a customer id.
To combine several commits into one. GitHub's Squash and merge button does this when it merges a pull request.
Secure Shell: a way to connect safely to another computer, or to GitHub, over a network, often with a key pair.
A customizable bar at the bottom of Codex. Run /statusline to choose its items, such as model, context and git.
A word after a program's name that picks what it does. In git commit, commit is the subcommand.
A Git repository placed inside another repository and fixed to one of its commits.
The rules for how code must be written: which words and symbols go where. A syntax error means a rule was broken.
Instructions sent to an AI model before your own messages. They set its role and rules, and you usually do not see them.
Pressing the Tab key to finish a file or command name that you started typing.
The extra work you create for later when you choose a quick, imperfect solution now.
The share of your code lines that run during tests. High coverage does not prove that the tests are good.
A way of working: write a failing test first, then write only enough code to make it pass.
A recorded date and time for an event, such as when a file or commit was made.
A file that Git already follows because it was added and committed. .gitignore does not affect tracked files.
The large collection of text and code that an AI model learned from. After training, the model does not search it.
A group of database changes that succeed or fail together. If one step fails, all the changes are undone.
To translate code from one language or version into another of a similar level, such as TypeScript into JavaScript.
A note in code that says what type a value should have. Python ignores it when running.
An error that means you used a value in a way its type does not allow, such as adding a number to text.
JavaScript with added type information. Files end in .ts. Tools translate it into plain JavaScript so that it can run.
User interface: everything on screen that a person sees and uses, such as buttons, menus and forms.
In JavaScript, the value of a variable that has no value yet, or of a property that does not exist.
Fixing a dependency to one exact version, such as 1.4.2, so that updates cannot change it by surprise.
A simulated computer running inside your real computer, kept apart from your own files.
A free code editor from Microsoft. The Codex IDE extension works beside your code; check its page for supported editors.
A weakness in software that an attacker could use to cause harm, such as stealing data.
In a web app, a rule that matches a URL, such as /about, to the code that answers it.
A URL that a service calls to tell your app that something happened, such as a new push to GitHub.
Another working folder with its own files and branch that shares one git repository. Codex can use worktrees to run chats in parallel.
Windows Subsystem for Linux: a Windows feature that runs a Linux system inside Windows, with its own terminal and files.
A shell that is the default in the macOS Terminal app for new accounts since macOS 10.15.
